subtitle: Where deeper industrial integration creates strategic value, through which instruments, and where to stay out

Battery Materials & Cells: Batteries assembly (Korea->Australia). Grid Equipment & Conductors: Power cables (Korea->Australia). Electric Vehicles: Electric Vehicles assembly (Korea->Australia).

Common anti-circumvention rules for solar refining (copper wire & rod, polysilicon) and batteries refining (battery materials (foil, electrolyte), cathode materials & precursors, cobalt intermediates & chemicals) and electric vehicles refining (rare-earth metals, rare-earth oxides & compounds). Bind market access for batteries assembly (li-ion cells & packs, other accumulators), batteries components (accumulator parts & separators), electric vehicles components (accumulator parts & separators, electric motors, ferrite & other magnets), wind towers, wind assembly (electricity meters, overhead conductors, power cables), power cables. Keep nuclear special materials; battery recycling feed; semiconductor manufacturing equipment open to global sourcing.
Upgrade EFA-KEXIM co-financing channel for critical minerals: sector strategy, reciprocal commitments, a KPI dashboard and an annual review. No new MOU.

Do not create a new bilateral energy MOU or a free-standing MEA institution. Do not put new public money behind Batteries extraction (cobalt ores, lithium minerals, natural graphite) investment that is already committed (evidence KRAU-14. Do not put new public money behind Batteries refining (battery materials (foil, electrolyte), cathode materials & precursors, cobalt intermediates & chemicals) investment that is already committed (evidence KRAU-11.

Of 142 technology x stage cells and electro-industrial nodes assessed for the pair, 25 show an active complementarity (a supplier meeting the other's need, a shared chokepoint, a capacity-constrained trusted supplier or a chain specialisation), 0 direct competition and 90 no strategic case. The relationship is not one of general similarity: most of the electro-industrial base needs no bilateral intervention.

AIB strategic roles: Korea Specialized Technology & Manufacturing Anchor (primary), Scale Manufacturing & Integration Platform (primary), Coordination / Bridge Hub (secondary), Capital & Investment Anchor (secondary); Australia Resource & Processing Anchor (primary).

Australia supplies rare-earth metals, lithium minerals where Korea is short; Korea supplies wind towers, power cables, cathode materials & precursors, accumulator parts & separators where Australia is short; they share no node-level chokepoint where neither supplies.

From the AIB roles, Korea brings specialised technology and manufacturing, scale manufacturing, coordination across allied chains; Australia brings resources and processing. Public finance runs through KEXIM, K-SURE, KOMIR, KDB on the Korea side and EFA, NRFC, CEFC, ARENA on the Australia side. The trade is market access and demand certainty for trusted capacity.

This section sets out what already exists before anything new is proposed. Facts are from the curated evidence layer (accessed 2026-11-06); items marked partial or unverified rest on secondary sources and should be confirmed before citation.
Australia's memberships in OSI's economic-security agreements table: IPEF, MSP, U.S. FTA.
DFAT notes RCEP entered into force for Korea on 1 Feb 2022 and may be used by exporters as an alternative to KAFTA; the member list shown here is partial.
Sixth 2+2 met 1 May 2024 with a joint statement; no 2025-26 meeting was found, and the biennial cadence implies the next falls around 2026.
Lee noted large Korean investment in Australian lithium, critical-minerals and rare-earth projects; no joint statement or deliverable found.
ASPI lists the MSP, which Korea chairs in 2025, among the frameworks for Australia-Korea minerals cooperation; Australian membership is not stated in that article.

Korea chaired the Minerals Security Partnership until June 2026; a February 2026 report says its 17 members carried into the successor FORGE; Korean public lenders joined the MSP Finance Network; no signed US-Korea critical-minerals MOU was found.

On 24 Jun 2026 Korea Zinc's chair met Albanese in Canberra on supply chains and smelting competitiveness and agreed to explore cooperation; Project Crucible is the US$7.4bn Tennessee smelter, not an Australian investment.
Albanese called Korea a trusted partner in critical minerals and clean energy at a Sep 2026 UNGA meeting, the third bilateral after the G7 and APEC; no deliverable reported; day approximate.
In the OSI energy basket, Korea imported US$18.1bn from Australia and Australia imported US$10.9bn from Korea (bilateral flows 2024, summed over the technology x stage cells).

Signed in Seoul 8 Apr 2014 and in force 12 Dec 2014; Australia reached duty-free on all Korean imports from 1 Jan 2021 and Korean tariffs on Australian goods were phased out by 2023; RCEP is an alternative route.
The 2021 partnership commits both to critical-mineral supply-chain resilience and a ministers' MoU, with a Critical Minerals Working Group on supply-chain mapping, R&D and investment.
Revised 1988 MOU signed 30 Oct 2025 at APEC Gyeongju names critical minerals and hydrogen, joint third-market entry and resumed biennial consultations in Australia from 2026.
Investment vehicle, project pipeline and financing
Australia announced an initial A$50m for the critical-minerals partnership, with Korea to match subject to domestic processes; USD value approximate.
EFA and the Export-Import Bank of Korea signed an MoU in Sep 2023 on co-financing in critical minerals and related sectors; no amounts given, and the day is approximate.
Corporate relationships in the recommended compacts
Binding term sheet Jan 2022 and full offtake May 2022 for spodumene concentrate; reported buyer termination right if production had not begun by 1 Sep 2025.
Oct 2022 five-year offtake (option for five more) with SK On taking a 10% stake in the ASX-listed Lake Resources.
Seven-year NdPr oxide offtake (600 t/yr rising to 1,500 t/yr) with conditions to be met by end-Jun 2026; KEXIM issued a letter of intent for up to US$150m debt.
Two Korean government-owned banks funded US$460m for the Gwangyang plant, non-recourse to Pilbara Minerals; date approximate.
Feb 2024 second agreement for up to 85,000 t of concentrate from Mt Holland, after a 2022 deal for 50,000 t of hydroxide; no value disclosed.
Nov 2024 agreement lets SK On take up to 15,000 t of Korea-made hydroxide from Australian-sourced spodumene; POSCO Future M is to take 20,000 t a year; day approximate.

Plant converts Pilgangoora spodumene to battery-grade hydroxide (43,000 t/yr nameplate); train 1 ramped in 2024 and train 2 was completed in early 2025; no 2026 production data found; day approximate.
ASM's Korean plant opened in 2022 and produces neodymium metals and alloys (designed 5,200 t/yr); its Dubbo (NSW) mine, intended to feed it, has unclear funding in the sources seen.
POSCO's 4 Sep 2026 release says it acquired a stake in a high-quality lithium mine owned by Mineral Resources in 2026; mine name, stake size and amount are not given.

Final investment decision in May 2026 after an Australian offtake commitment under the Strategic Reserve; construction began 8 Oct 2026; credit agencies from the US, Canada, Korea and Germany support it; the article's A$1.2bn figure is ambiguous.
Unverified items are left out of this section; they stay in the evidence register (evidence_register.csv) and the evidence layer.

Working channels today: Comprehensive Strategic Partnership and Critical Minerals Working Group (finance); EFA-KEXIM co-financing channel for critical minerals (a project pipeline and finance). What the relationship lacks: no cross-sector KPI dashboard or review cycle; KRAU-M3 has no published project pipeline.

Every recommendation (IDs J, C, T, I, X, D, N, M) has rows in evidence_register.csv: the OSI metrics behind it (variable, value for each country, year, source, evidence specificity) and any external items, with URL and access date. Recommendations that rest on external research only carry basis = external.
External evidence vintage: accessed 2026-11-06; 256 items (partial 197, unverified 18, verified 41).
Where the findings are weak or counterintuitive
Joint bets resting on a node need inherited from its cell (a proxy): Wind towers; Power cables.
Evidence-led compacts (OSI cannot see the partner's capability in trade data): Battery Materials & Cells; Permanent Magnets & Drive Systems.

Australia has no listed trade position (under 1% of world supply) at nodes where Korea has material demand: wafers, polysilicon, synthetic graphite (anode-grade), rare-earth oxides & compounds, natural graphite, battery materials (foil, electrolyte), battery recycling feed, electric motors, rare-earth permanent magnets, electric buses, trucks & tractors, pv cover glass, automatic controllers, ac generators, refrigerants, graphite electrodes, semiconductor manufacturing equipment, hydrogen, ammonia & methanol, nuclear special materials, silver powder, direct-reduced iron (dri/hbi). Trade data miss capability that is owned abroad or sold at home, so these nodes cannot show complementarity even where corporate evidence suggests it.
Low-evidence units among the active states: none.

Fuel-trade lanes reach tier 1 (coal refining; buyer: both): real energy-security lanes, but outside the electro-industrial compacts and with no market failure beyond the supply concentration the engine measures.
